config.title: Nested Routes & Protected Routes

intro.title: Nested Routes & Protected Routes
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple dashboard application with a login page and a main content area. You will learn how to organize your app's pages using nested routes, where some components are displayed inside others based on the URL. To secure parts of the app, you will implement protected routes that check for user authentication before allowing access. The main technologies you'll use are React Router for navigation and TypeScript for adding type safety to your components and routes.
intro.usecase: Nested and protected routes are essential for building secure, organized applications with complex navigation structures. You'll see this pattern in admin dashboards where different sections (users, analytics, settings) are nested under a main layout, while authentication protects sensitive areas. E-commerce platforms use nested routes for product categories/subcategories and protect checkout pages from unauthorized access. Social media apps nest profile content under user pages and protect direct messaging features. Mastering these concepts lets you create professional applications with proper access control and logical information architecture.

objectives: Apply React Router's Route component to define parent routes that serve as layout containers
Use the Outlet component to render nested child routes within parent route layouts
Implement a ProtectedRoute component to control access to routes based on authentication state
Execute conditional rendering within route components to display different UI based on user permissions
Utilize the useNavigate hook to programmatically redirect users when authentication checks fail
Construct nested route structures with multiple levels of parent-child relationships
Define route parameters within nested routes to access dynamic segments at different levels
Handle authentication state in a React context or state management solution to share across protected routes
Apply TypeScript interfaces to type-check route parameters and authentication props
Implement route configuration patterns that separate public routes from protected route hierarchies
Use React Router's index routes to define default content for nested route paths
Modify existing route structures to add new nested routes without breaking existing navigation

steps.title: Import React and React Router DOM
steps.instruction: Import React from 'react' and BrowserRouter, Routes, Route, Link from 'react-router-dom'.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in the necessary modules. Remember to import React for JSX and the routing components for navigation.
steps.seedCode: // Import React and React Router DOM components here
steps.expectedOutcome: The imports are added at the top of the file, making React and the routing components available for use.
successCriteria: The code includes import statements for React and the specified react-router-dom components.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and the routing components. This sets up the foundation for building routes in your application.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you've imported all the required components: React, BrowserRouter, Routes, Route, and Link.
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports are missing or incorrect. Make sure to import React from 'react' and BrowserRouter, Routes, Route, Link from 'react-router-dom'.

steps.title: Create the main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns a BrowserRouter wrapper. The component should be typed to return JSX.Element.
steps.hint: Define the App component using either a function declaration or arrow function syntax. Make sure it returns a BrowserRouter element.
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional App component is defined that returns a BrowserRouter wrapper.
successCriteria: BrowserRouter is used as the root element
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the App component with proper TypeScript typing and BrowserRouter structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: Did you name the component 'App'? Does it return a BrowserRouter element? Is it typed to return JSX.Element?
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component isn't properly defined. Make sure to create a functional component named App that returns a BrowserRouter element.

steps.title: Create a Dashboard component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named Dashboard that returns a simple div element containing the text 'Dashboard'.
steps.hint: You can create a component using either a function declaration or an arrow function. Make sure to return JSX.
steps.expectedOutcome: A Dashboard component is created that renders a div with 'Dashboard' text.
successCriteria: The Dashboard component is defined, returns JSX, and contains the text 'Dashboard' inside a div element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the Dashboard component. This will serve as the parent component for nested routes.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there might be a small issue. Make sure your component returns a div element containing exactly the text 'Dashboard'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Dashboard component isn't quite right. Check that you've created a component named Dashboard that returns a div with 'Dashboard' text.

steps.title: Create nested route components
steps.instruction: Create two functional components named Profile and Settings. Each component should return a simple heading element with text indicating its purpose.
steps.hint:
Define Profile and Settings as separate components that return JSX elements like

Profile

and

Settings

.
steps.expectedOutcome: Two new components (Profile and Settings) are defined, each returning a heading element with appropriate text.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the Profile and Settings components that will serve as nested routes under Dashboard.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've created both Profile and Settings components, each returning a heading element.
steps.feedbackWrong: Please create two separate components named Profile and Settings that return simple heading elements.

steps.title: Set up basic routing structure
steps.instruction: Inside the App component, add a Routes component and a Route component that renders the Dashboard component when the path is '/dashboard'.
steps.hint: Import Routes and Route from 'react-router-dom', then use them inside the BrowserRouter in your App component.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component now contains a basic routing structure with Routes and Route components that will render the Dashboard component at '/dashboard'.
successCriteria: Add Route component with path='/dashboard' and element={<Dashboard />}
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully set up the basic routing structure with Routes and Route components. The Dashboard component will now render when navigating to '/dashboard'.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but something is missing. Make sure you've imported Routes and Route, added the Routes component inside BrowserRouter, and created a Route with path='/dashboard' that renders the Dashboard component.
steps.feedbackWrong: The routing structure isn't set up correctly. You need to import Routes and Route from 'react-router-dom', then use them inside the BrowserRouter to create a route for the Dashboard component at '/dashboard'.

steps.title: Implement nested routing in Dashboard
steps.hint: Add an import statement for Outlet from the same package you imported BrowserRouter from.
steps.analogousExample:
// Import Outlet from react-router-dom
import { Outlet } from 'react-router-dom';
steps.expectedOutcome: The Outlet component is imported and ready to be used for nested routing.
successCriteria: The import statement for Outlet from 'react-router-dom' is added to the code.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported the Outlet component, which will serve as a placeholder for rendering nested route components.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're importing Outlet from 'react-router-dom'.
steps.feedbackWrong: This step requires importing the Outlet component from 'react-router-dom'. Check the import statement syntax.

steps.title: Add navigation links for nested routes
steps.instruction: In the Dashboard component, add two Link components from react-router-dom to navigate to '/dashboard/profile' and '/dashboard/settings'. Place them inside the existing h1 element.
steps.hint: Import Link from react-router-dom and use it like <Link to="/path">Link Text</Link>.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Dashboard component will have navigation links that allow users to switch between the nested profile and settings routes.
successCriteria: Add at least two Link components inside Dashboard
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added navigation links to the nested routes. Users can now click these links to navigate between the profile and settings pages.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've imported Link from react-router-dom and created links to both '/dashboard/profile' and '/dashboard/settings'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Dashboard component should include navigation links. Import Link from react-router-dom and create two Link components with the correct paths.

steps.title: Create a ProtectedRoute component
steps.instruction: Create a new functional component named ProtectedRoute that accepts props: children and isAuthenticated. The component should return the children if isAuthenticated is true, otherwise return a message indicating the user is not authenticated.
steps.hint: Define a component that takes props with TypeScript types. Use conditional rendering to check isAuthenticated.
steps.expectedOutcome: A ProtectedRoute component is created that conditionally renders children based on isAuthenticated.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the ProtectedRoute component with proper TypeScript props and conditional rendering.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your ProtectedRoute component accepts both children and isAuthenticated props and uses them in conditional rendering.
steps.feedbackWrong: The ProtectedRoute component is missing or doesn't meet the requirements. It should be a functional component that takes children and isAuthenticated props and conditionally renders based on authentication status.

steps.title: Add authentication state
steps.instruction: In the App component, initialize a state variable named isAuthenticated using useState. Set its initial value to false and use the boolean type.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook with a generic type parameter <boolean> to create a boolean state variable.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will have a boolean state variable isAuthenticated initialized to false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the authentication state to the App component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've used useState with the boolean type and named the variable isAuthenticated with an initial value of false.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. In the App component, use useState<boolean>(false) to create an isAuthenticated state variable.

steps.title: Implement ProtectedRoute logic
steps.instruction: Create the ProtectedRoute component with conditional rendering logic that returns its children if isAuthenticated is true, otherwise returns a redirect to a login page.
steps.hint: Define a function component named ProtectedRoute that takes props (including children). Use a conditional statement to check the isAuthenticated state and return either the children or a redirect.
steps.expectedOutcome: A ProtectedRoute component is defined that conditionally renders children or redirects based on authentication status.
successCriteria: Returns Navigate to "/login" if not authenticated
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented the ProtectedRoute component with conditional rendering logic.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your ProtectedRoute component correctly checks isAuthenticated and returns either the children or a Navigate component to "/login".
steps.feedbackWrong: The ProtectedRoute component is not implemented correctly. It should be a function component that takes children as a prop and conditionally renders them based on isAuthenticated.

steps.title: Create a Login component
steps.instruction: Create a new functional component named Login that returns a heading and a button. The button should have text 'Login'.
steps.hint: Define a function called Login that returns JSX with an h1 and a button element.
steps.expectedOutcome: A Login component is created with a heading and a login button.
successCriteria: Returns JSX with h1 and button
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the Login component with the required structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your Login component returns an h1 heading and a button with the text 'Login'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Login component is missing or doesn't have the correct structure. Create a function named Login that returns JSX with an h1 and a button.

steps.title: Wire authentication toggling
steps.instruction: In the Login component, add an onClick handler to the button that toggles the isAuthenticated state using its setter function.
steps.hint: The Login component already has a button element. Add an onClick prop to it that calls a function to toggle the authentication state.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Login button will now toggle the authentication state when clicked, enabling the protected routes functionality.
successCriteria: Login component has a button with onClick handler
Handler uses setIsAuthenticated from App component
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've successfully wired the Login button to toggle the authentication state. This will allow users to log in and access protected routes.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there are a few issues. Make sure the onClick handler properly toggles the isAuthenticated state using its setter function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button isn't properly wired to toggle authentication. Check that you've added an onClick handler that calls setIsAuthenticated with the toggled value.

steps.title: Protect the Dashboard route
steps.instruction: In the App component, wrap the Dashboard Route with the ProtectedRoute component and pass the isAuthenticated prop to it.
steps.hint: The ProtectedRoute component expects an isAuthenticated prop to determine if the user is authenticated. Wrap the Route element that renders the Dashboard component inside ProtectedRoute.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of wrapping a Route with a ProtectedRoute
<ProtectedRoute isAuthenticated={isAuthenticated}>
  <Route path="/dashboard" element={<Dashboard />} />
</ProtectedRoute>
steps.expectedOutcome: The Dashboard route is now protected and will redirect to the login page if the user is not authenticated.
successCriteria: isAuthenticated prop is passed to ProtectedRoute
Dashboard Route is wrapped inside ProtectedRoute
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully wrapped the Dashboard route with the ProtectedRoute component, passing the isAuthenticated state. This ensures only authenticated users can access the Dashboard.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to wrap the Dashboard Route with ProtectedRoute and pass the isAuthenticated prop correctly.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Dashboard route is not properly protected. Ensure you wrap the Route element for Dashboard with the ProtectedRoute component and pass the isAuthenticated prop.
